newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mitsubishi says new engine will power most cars.
newsitem.headline: Mitsubishi says new engine will power most cars.

text.p: Mitsubishi Motors Corp said on Tuesday its direct injection petrol engine will become the standard power plant for cars in the twenty-first century.

Mitsubishi said the new engine, thanks to improvements in engine management computer systems to tightly control the burning of fuel, is more efficient than a diesel, but without loosing the petrol engine's advantage in power.
Mitsubishi's Kiyotaka Takizawa told a press conference at the Paris Car Show that the company started selling cars in Japan with the new engine last month.
Mitsubishi said it is the first company in the world to include a direct-injection petrol motor as an option. The company believes it has a start of up to four years on its competitors.
Takizawa, Corporate General Manager at Mitsubishi cars, said the new engine is a practical realisation of what engineers had long dreamed about.

"This is an engine where gasoline is directly injected into the cylinder. Fuel injection during the late stage of the compression stroke was once impossible, However, new advanced technology... has enabled combustion of an ultra-lean mixture," Takizawa said.
"As a result, an engine that offers high performance, yet is cleaner and very fuel efficient has been realized," Takizawa said.
Mitsubishi, which has launched the new engine in a 1.8 litre 4-cylinder version of its Galant family car, has an array of claims for the system:
- A 25 percent improvement in fuel economy in town driving.
- Eight percent more economical than conventional engines at 75 miles per hour.

Mitsubishi says that compared with a diesel engine of a comparable capacity the new engine produces about seven per cent better fuel economy, 85 percent more power, zero particulate emissions, lower noise levels at all speeds, it weighs eight percent less and costs 40 percent less to produce.

Automotive industry analysts believe all the major manufacturers are hurridly working on matching the Mitsubishi technology. Toyota Motor Corp of Japan has already announced plans to offer a direct injection car later this year.
But they point out that so-called breakthroughs in the past have failed to deliver and that the progress of the new engines will be watched closely.

About 10 years ago, German mass car maker Volkswagen said its engineers had produced a direct injection petrol engine, but it never found its way onto the showroom floor. VW could reproduce all the advantages in efficiency, but could not overcome the problem of reliability.
